title: The surah opens with one name: the Most Merciful.
subtitle: Everything that follows flows from His mercy
then: Maududi says the title deeply fits the surah, because from beginning to end it lists {idea}the fruits of Allah's mercy and grace{/idea}. Ibn Kathir records that the Prophet ﷺ recited it to his companions and they were silent, and said {reward}the jinn had answered better{/reward}.
now: You open your phone and the first thing you see is a bill, a bad headline, a message from your boss. Your day starts with pressure. {idea}This surah starts with mercy{/idea}, and asks you to read everything after it in that light.
old: My day is mostly about problems to solve.
new: Everything I have comes from the Most Merciful, before any problem.
try: Start tomorrow morning by saying Ar-Rahman once, slowly, before you look at your phone.

title: His first named gift is that He taught the Quran.
subtitle: Before sun and earth, the gift of guidance

row.title: the Quran
sub: made easy to learn and memorize

then: Ibn Kathir says Allah begins by telling of His mercy: He revealed the Quran and {reward}made memorizing and understanding it easy{/reward} for those He has mercy on. In the list of favors, {idea}the Quran comes even before man is mentioned{/idea}.
now: You learned a short surah as a child, maybe from a grandparent, maybe in a cold mosque classroom. You still know it by heart. {reward}That was Ar-Rahman teaching you{/reward}, through the people He sent.
old: I learned the Quran because someone made me.
new: Every verse I know is a gift taught to me by the Most Merciful.
try: Recite one surah you know by heart, slowly, and thank Allah for teaching it to you.

title: He created the human being.
subtitle: You exist because He chose to make you
then: Three short lines open the surah: {idea}Ar-Rahman, taught the Quran, created man{/idea}. Ibn Kathir reads them together as Allah telling of His favors. The human being is named as one of the mercies, {reward}made to carry that teaching{/reward}.
now: You look in the mirror and see tired eyes, extra weight, grey hair. You compare yourself to someone online. {idea}Before any of that, you were made on purpose{/idea}, by the One whose first name here is mercy.
old: I am just one more person among billions.
new: I was created by the Most Merciful. That is my first identity.
try: Look in the mirror once today and say: Allah made me. Then thank Him.

title: He taught him to speak clearly.
subtitle: The gift of words
then: Al-Hasan said al-bayan means {reward}eloquent speech{/reward}. Ibn Kathir links it to the Quran: Allah taught people how to recite by {idea}making it easy to pronounce letters{/idea} with the tongue, the lips and the parts of the mouth.
now: You hear a toddler say her first words, or a stroke patient work hard for one sentence. Then you think of how easily you talk all day, in voice notes and meetings and arguments. {idea}Every word is borrowed.{/idea}
old: Talking is just something everyone can do.
new: My ability to speak is a taught gift, and I will be asked how I used it.
try: Use your words today to say one kind, specific thing to someone.

title: The sun and moon run on exact calculation.
subtitle: Precision you set your clock by
then: Ibn Kathir says they move {idea}according to precise calculation that is never delayed nor disturbed{/idea}. He cites the verse that the sun does not overtake the moon, each floating in its orbit, and that this is {reward}the measuring of the Almighty, the All-Knowing{/reward}.
now: Your prayer app knows exactly when Fajr is tomorrow, and next year. You plan Ramadan by the moon. {idea}You live by the sky's timetable without ever thanking its Maker.{/idea}
old: Sunrise and sunset are just background.
new: Every exact sunrise is a favor and a sign from the One who measured it.
try: Watch the sunset today, or check its exact time, and say SubhanAllah.

title: The stars and the trees bow down.
subtitle: All of creation in prostration
then: Ibn Kathir notes two views on an-najm: {idea}plants that lie on the ground{/idea}, or the stars in the sky, which he calls most obvious. He cites the verse that everything in the heavens and earth, sun, moon, stars, mountains, trees, {reward}prostrates to Allah{/reward}, and many people too.
now: You walk past a tree on your street every day without looking up. It is doing what it was made for. {idea}The stars over your roof are doing the same.{/idea} The question is whether you are.
old: Trees and stars are just scenery.
new: All of creation bows to Allah. My prayer joins something already happening.
try: Pray one prayer today thinking of the trees and stars bowing with you.

title: He raised the sky and set the balance.
subtitle: The universe is built on justice
then: Ibn Kathir says the balance here means {idea}justice{/idea}. He cites the verse that Allah sent messengers with the Book and the balance {reward}so that people may keep up equity{/reward}. The same Lord who raised the sky set fairness into creation.
now: You notice it in your body when something is unfair: the colleague who takes credit, the sibling who gets the bigger share. That ache is not random. {idea}You were made to recognize the balance.{/idea}
old: Fairness is just a human idea.
new: Justice is built into creation, set by the One who raised the sky.
try: Notice one place in your day where you can be fairer than you need to be.

title: So that you do not cross the line of the balance.
subtitle: The purpose of justice in creation
then: Ibn Kathir explains that Allah {idea}created the heavens and earth in justice and truth{/idea} so that everything stands on justice. The command follows: {trap}do not transgress the balance{/trap}. The order of the sky is a lesson for the person.
now: You split the restaurant bill and slip in a little less than your share. You speak over someone in a meeting. {trap}Small crossings of the line{/trap} that nobody calls out. {idea}The whole universe stays inside its line.{/idea}
old: A little unfairness here and there does not matter.
new: The universe keeps its balance. I am asked to keep mine.
try: Pay or give your full fair share in one shared thing today.

title: Weigh fairly and do not short the scale.
subtitle: Justice in everyday dealings

row.title: in every exchange
sub: a sale, a deal, a share

then: Ibn Kathir says this means {trap}do not cheat in weights and measures{/trap}, but observe justice and fairness. He cites the verse: {idea}weigh with the true and straight balance{/idea}. The cosmic balance comes down to the market stall.
now: You sell a used car and stay quiet about the noise in the engine. You bill a client for an hour you did not work. You give someone a review that is not true. {idea}Every honest deal keeps the balance Allah set.{/idea}
old: Business is business. Everyone bends a little.
new: Honesty in a small deal is part of the balance that holds up the sky.
try: In your next sale, invoice or trade, tell the whole truth about what you are giving.

title: He laid out the earth for all creatures.
subtitle: A stable home shared by every kind
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah laid the earth and {idea}balanced it with firm mountains{/idea} so that it would be stable for its residents. Al-anam means the creatures, {reward}different in species, shape, color and language{/reward}.
now: You stand on solid ground every day and never think about it, until an earthquake on the news reminds you. You share the street with neighbors who speak other languages, and birds and cats. {reward}The ground under all of you is one gift.{/reward}
old: The ground is just there.
new: The stable earth under my feet is a gift laid out for every creature.
try: Walk outside barefoot or on grass for a minute today and thank Allah for solid ground.

title: Fruit, and palm trees with dates in their sheaths.
subtitle: Food wrapped and ripened for you

key.label: What I see in a fruit

then: Ibn Kathir says the fruits come in {reward}various colors, tastes and scents{/reward}. The date palm is named specifically {idea}because of its benefit, both fresh and dry{/idea}. Its sheathed stalks grow seeds into clusters that ripen, then ripen more.
now: You grab a banana from the bowl on your way out, half-awake, eating while you answer emails. Somewhere a tree spent months making it, wrapped and timed for you. {reward}Every fruit is a small letter of mercy.{/reward}
old: Fruit is just something I buy at the shop.
new: Every fruit is grown, wrapped and ripened by the Most Merciful.
try: Eat one piece of fruit slowly today and say Alhamdulillah after it.

title: Grain with its husk, and fragrant plants.
subtitle: Even the straw and the scent are gifts
then: Ibn Abbas said al-asf is {reward}straw{/reward}, the dried leaves around the grain. Rayhan was explained as green leaves, or by Al-Hasan as {reward}sweet-scented plants{/reward}. Ibn Kathir says the meaning is crops like wheat and barley and the leaves on their stems.
now: You eat bread every day. You smell basil or mint and feel calmer for a second. You never think about the straw that fed the cow that gave the milk. {idea}The favor reaches further than the part you see.{/idea}
old: Bread is just bread.
new: Grain, husk and fragrance are a whole chain of favors.
try: Before your next meal with bread or rice, pause and name where it came from.

title: Which of your Lord's favors would you deny?
subtitle: The first refrain, after Quran, speech, sky, balance and food
then: Ibn Kathir says the question is to {idea}mankind and jinn{/idea}: which of the favors that surround you do you deny? The Prophet ﷺ said the jinn answered each time: {reward}none of Your favors do we deny, our Lord, all praise is Yours{/reward}.
now: You are surrounded right now: a body that speaks, a sky that keeps time, food in the kitchen. You complain about the Wi-Fi. {idea}The question is not whether you have favors, but whether you admit them.{/idea}
old: I do not deny Allah's favors. I just do not think about them.
new: Forgetting a favor is a quiet way of denying it.
try: When you hear this verse recited, answer quietly: none of Your favors do I deny.

title: He made the human from dry clay, like pottery.
subtitle: Humble material, careful hands
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah created mankind {idea}from clay like that used in pottery{/idea}. He cites the hadith in Muslim that angels were made of light, jinn of smokeless fire, and {reward}Adam from what was described to you{/reward}.
now: You hold a clay mug in the morning. Ordinary mud, made useful by someone's hands. You feel worthless after a hard week, or proud after a promotion. {idea}Both forget the same thing: you are clay shaped by Allah.{/idea}
old: My worth depends on how well I am doing.
new: I am humble clay, and my value is that Allah shaped me.
try: Hold a cup or bowl today and remember what you are made from. Say Alhamdulillah.

title: And the jinn He made from smokeless flame.
subtitle: The other audience of this surah
then: Ibn Abbas said the jinn were created {idea}from the tip of the flame of a smokeless fire{/idea}, from its best part. This is why the refrain says {reward}your Lord, you two{/reward}: it speaks to humans and jinn together.
now: You think you are the only kind of being trying to live right. This verse reminds you that another creation, unseen, hears the same question. {reward}The jinn answered well when it was recited.{/reward} You can too.
old: This surah is talking only to people like me.
new: Two kinds of creation hear the same question about Allah's favors.
try: Next time you hear Surah Ar-Rahman, answer each refrain the way the jinn did.

title: Clay and fire both made. Which favor would you deny?
subtitle: The refrain after the creation of humans and jinn
then: The refrain comes right after the creation of {idea}humans from clay and jinn from fire{/idea}. The favor in view is existence itself. Neither creation asked to be made, and both were {reward}given form, life and purpose{/reward}.
now: Your birthday comes and you think about age and what you have not done yet. You rarely stop on the plain fact: {reward}you exist at all{/reward}. Someone chose that. {idea}It is the favor under every other favor.{/idea}
old: Being alive is just the starting point, not a gift.
new: That I exist at all is the first favor I can never deny.
try: Take one deep breath today and thank Allah simply for making you.

title: Lord of the two sunrises and the two sunsets.
subtitle: The sun's path shifting through the year
then: Ibn Kathir says this means {idea}the sunrise of summer and winter, and the sunset of summer and winter{/idea}. He cites the verse: the Lord of the east and west, so {reward}take Him alone as your trustee{/reward}. The variation brings benefits to all creation.
now: You notice it gets dark at five in winter and you feel low. In summer the evenings stretch out. Your moods follow the seasons. {idea}The One who moves the sunrise along the horizon does not change{/idea}, whatever season you are in.
old: Seasons just happen, and I put up with them.
new: Every season is managed by one Lord I can trust in all of them.
try: Notice where the sun rises or sets from your window this week. Remember its Lord.

title: Summer and winter both. Which favor would you deny?
subtitle: The refrain after the two sunrises and sunsets
then: Ibn Kathir explains the two easts and wests with {reward}the benefits this variation brings{/reward} to humans and jinn. Then the refrain: {idea}which of these favors would you deny?{/idea} The changing year is a gift, not an accident.
now: You complain in July that it is too hot and in January that it is too cold. Meanwhile, the wheat ripens in one and the ground rests in the other. {reward}The change you grumble about is feeding you.{/reward}
old: I would prefer if the weather stayed the same.
new: The turning of the seasons is a favor I live on.
try: The next time you complain about the weather, stop and name one good thing it brings.

title: He let two seas flow, meeting side by side.
subtitle: Fresh water and salt water, released together
then: Ibn Abbas said maraja means {idea}He let them loose{/idea}. Ibn Kathir says the two seas are {reward}the fresh and the salty waters{/reward}, the fresh coming from rivers. He links it to the verse in Al-Furqan about one sweet, one bitter.
now: You turn on the tap and drink fresh water, while the ocean you swam in last summer would make you sick. Both sit on the same planet. {idea}Someone keeps your water drinkable.{/idea}
old: Fresh water is just what comes out of the tap.
new: Drinkable water beside an ocean of salt is a sign of careful design.
try: Drink a glass of water slowly today and thank Allah that it is sweet.

title: A barrier between them, and neither crosses over.
subtitle: Each keeps what it was made to be
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah placed a barrier between the two waters {idea}so that they do not transgress upon each other{/idea}, which would {trap}spoil the characteristics they were created with{/trap}. Neither overruns the other.
now: You need boundaries too: work that does not swallow your evenings, a phone that does not come to bed, a friend whose bad habits do not become yours. {idea}Boundaries keep you who you are.{/idea}
old: Boundaries are walls that keep people out.
new: A barrier can be a mercy that keeps two good things from spoiling each other.
try: Set one small boundary today, like no phone during one meal.

title: Two waters kept apart. Which favor would you deny?
subtitle: The refrain after the barrier between the seas
then: After describing the barrier that keeps {idea}fresh and salt water from spoiling each other{/idea}, the refrain returns. The favor is the protection itself: rivers and wells that {reward}stay drinkable{/reward} beside the salty sea.
now: You only notice the barrier when it fails: a drought on the news, a flood that turns a town's water brown, a boil-water notice. {reward}Most days it just works.{/reward} {idea}That is the favor.{/idea}
old: I will notice water when there is a problem with it.
new: Water that works every day is a protection I should thank Allah for daily.
try: Make wudu slowly once today, feeling the water, and thank Allah for it.

title: From both seas come pearls and coral.
subtitle: Beauty brought out of the deep
then: Ibn Kathir notes views that marjan means {reward}small pearls{/reward}, or large precious ones. Ibn Abbas said when it rains, oysters open their mouths and {idea}the drops that fall in turn into pearls{/idea}. Adornment is named as a favor.
now: You see a pearl in a shop window or on your mother's wedding necklace. Or just the shine of the sea at sunset. {reward}Allah did not only give you what you need. He gave you beautiful things too.{/reward}
old: Beauty is extra, not really a blessing.
new: Allah gives beauty on purpose, and it is a favor to notice.
try: Notice one beautiful thing today and say MashaAllah, it is from Allah.

title: Pearls from the deep. Which favor would you deny?
subtitle: The refrain after pearls and coral

row.title: the Lord
sub: who made it in the sea

then: Ibn Kathir says that since this kind of adornment is {reward}a favor from Allah to the people of earth{/reward}, He reminds them of it and asks again: {idea}which of these favors would you deny?{/idea}
now: You get a gift: a ring, a watch, a nice bottle of perfume. You thank the person, maybe post a photo. {idea}Behind the giver is the Giver{/idea}, who made the pearl in an oyster before any shop existed.
old: Nice things come from shops and money.
new: Every beautiful thing I own was first made by Allah.
try: Look at one thing you own that you find beautiful, and thank Allah before the person who gave it.

title: His are the ships, raised on the sea like mountains.
subtitle: Trade and travel carried on water

row.title: His
sub: and to Him belong the ships

then: Mujahid said the munsha'at are {idea}ships that hoist a sail{/idea}. Ibn Kathir says they are like mountains in size, and they make {reward}trade possible{/reward}, carrying cargo from one land to another so people get the goods they need.
now: Your phone, your shoes, the rice in your cupboard probably crossed an ocean in a container ship you will never see. {idea}The sea carries your daily life{/idea}, and the verse says those ships belong to Allah.
old: Things just arrive in shops.
new: Even the ships that bring my food and goods belong to Allah.
try: Check where one item in your home was made, and thank Allah for the journey it took.

title: Ships that carry your needs. Which favor would you deny?
subtitle: The refrain after the ships at sea

row.title: a sea that holds them up

then: Ibn Kathir says ships provide {reward}various benefits for people{/reward}, including carrying the goods they need. So, he says, the question comes again: {idea}which of your Lord's favors would you deny?{/idea}
now: You track a parcel online and watch it cross the sea. You never think about the water holding up thousands of tons of steel. {reward}Every delivery rides on a favor.{/reward}
old: Shipping is just logistics.
new: A sea that holds up ships for my sake is a favor I would be wrong to deny.
try: When your next delivery arrives, say Alhamdulillah before you open it.

title: Everyone on the earth will pass away.
subtitle: After all the favors, a reminder that they end
then: Qatadah said Allah {idea}first mentioned His creatures, then said all of this will perish{/idea}. Ash-Sha'bi advised that when you recite this verse, {reward}do not stop there{/reward}, continue to the next one about what remains.
now: You are at a funeral, or scrolling past news of someone your age who died. For a moment everything feels pointless. {idea}Do not stop at that thought.{/idea} The next verse is already waiting.
old: If everything ends, nothing really matters.
new: Everything passes so that I hold on to the One who does not.
try: Make a short dua today for someone who has passed away.

title: Only your Lord's Face remains, full of majesty and honor.
subtitle: What lasts when everything else ends
then: Ibn Kathir says only Allah's Face remains, because {idea}He is the Ever Living who never dies{/idea}. He links it to those who call on their Lord {reward}seeking His Face{/reward}, and those who feed others saying, we feed you only for Allah's Face.
now: You do a favor for a neighbor and wait for thanks that never comes. You post something good and count the likes. {idea}All of that fades.{/idea} Doing it for His Face is the only version that lasts.
old: If nobody notices what I do, it was wasted.
new: What I do for Allah's Face is the only thing that will not perish.
try: Do one kind act today purely for Allah, and tell no one.

title: A Lord who never dies. Which favor would you deny?
subtitle: The refrain after everything perishes except Him
then: Ibn Kathir says after stating that everyone on earth will die and return to {idea}Dhul-Jalal wal-Ikram{/idea}, who will {reward}judge them by His fair judgement{/reward}, Allah asks again which of His favors they would deny.
now: You sit in a hospital corridor waiting for news of someone you love. Everything feels fragile. {reward}The One who never dies is still there{/reward}, and no injustice in this world goes unjudged by Him.
old: Death is just loss.
new: That my Lord never dies and judges fairly is a favor in the face of every loss.
try: Say Ya Hayyu Ya Qayyum three times today when you feel anxious.

title: Everyone in heaven and earth asks Him. Every day He acts.
subtitle: All creation in need, and Allah never idle

row.title: His daily affair
sub: He answers the one who asks

then: Ibn Kathir says Allah is {idea}free of need{/idea} while every creature needs Him, willingly or not. Ubayd bin Umayr said of His daily affairs: {reward}He answers the one who calls, gives to the one who asks, removes hardship, cures the one seeking a cure{/reward}.
now: Right now, millions are asking Him: a student before an exam, a mother in labor, a farmer looking at the sky. You think your small request will get lost. {idea}Answering is what He does, every day.{/idea}
old: My small problems are not worth bringing to Allah.
new: Every day He is busy answering, giving and healing. My request is welcome.
try: Ask Allah today for one small, specific thing you need.

title: He answers every day. Which favor would you deny?
subtitle: The refrain after all creation asks Him
then: The refrain follows the picture of {idea}everyone in the heavens and earth asking Him{/idea}, and Him attending to an affair every day. The favor is that {reward}the door to ask is always open{/reward}.
now: You leave a message on a customer service line and wait three days. You text a friend and get left on read. {reward}With Allah you never wait in a queue.{/reward} {idea}Forgetting to ask is the only way to miss it.{/idea}
old: When I need help, I have to find someone with time for me.
new: My Lord has time for me every day. That is a favor I cannot deny.
try: Pick a fixed moment today, like after a prayer, just to ask Allah for what you need.

title: We will attend to you, O two weighty races.
subtitle: A day of reckoning for humans and jinn
then: Ibn Jurayj said it means {idea}We shall judge you{/idea}, and Al-Bukhari said, We shall repay you, adding that {reward}nothing keeps Allah from attending to anything else{/reward}. It is an Arabic way of speaking. Ath-thaqalan means humans and jinn.
now: You assume what you did last week is lost in the noise of eight billion people. Nobody important noticed. {idea}The verse says you will be personally attended to.{/idea} That is serious, and it also means you matter.
old: I am too small for my deeds to really be looked at.
new: Allah will attend to me personally. My life is not lost in the crowd.
try: Look back over yesterday and ask: what would I want to show Allah from it?

title: Told in advance. Which favor would you deny?
subtitle: The refrain after the promise of reckoning

row.title: a mercy
sub: told before it is too late

then: Ibn Kathir says Allah's {idea}warnings against His punishment{/idea} should move creatures to leave disobedience, and {reward}this is why He reminds them of it as a favor{/reward}. Being told about the reckoning before it comes is itself a gift.
now: Your manager tells you a week early that the audit is coming. You are annoyed, then relieved: at least there is time. {reward}Allah told you about the reckoning in your lifetime.{/reward} {idea}That is the head start.{/idea}
old: Hearing about judgement only makes me anxious.
new: Being warned while I can still change is a favor.
try: Fix one thing today you would not want to face unprepared.

title: Escape the heavens and earth if you can. You cannot.
subtitle: No way out of Allah's rule, except by His leave
then: Ibn Kathir says it means {idea}you will never escape Allah's decree{/idea}, which surrounds you wherever you are. On the Day of Gathering, angels will surround creation in seven rows. He cites: on that Day man will say, {trap}where is the escape? No refuge{/trap}.
now: You move cities, change your number, start a new job to leave a mistake behind. It follows you in your head. {idea}You cannot run from Allah, but you can always run to Him.{/idea}
old: If I get far enough away, I can leave it all behind.
new: There is no escape from Allah, only refuge with Him.
try: Turn to Allah today about the thing you have been trying to run from.

title: No way out but to Him. Which favor would you deny?
subtitle: The refrain after the challenge to escape

row.title: being held
sub: by a Lord who warns first

then: After the challenge to {idea}pass beyond the regions of the heavens and earth{/idea}, the refrain returns. Ibn Kathir says the warnings in these verses are meant to {reward}turn creatures away from disobedience{/reward}, which is why they are called favors.
now: A child who knows the rules of the house feels safer than one who does not. You know where all roads end. {reward}That clarity lets you stop running and start walking toward Him.{/reward}
old: Knowing I cannot escape feels like a trap.
new: Knowing where every road ends is a favor that helps me choose mine.
try: Write down one direction you want to walk toward Allah this month.

title: Flame and smoke sent on them, and no one to help.
subtitle: What meets those who try to flee on that Day
then: Ibn Abbas said shuwaz is {trap}the flame of fire{/trap}, and nuhas its smoke; others said molten brass. Ibn Kathir explains that if humans and jinn try to escape on the Day, angels will turn them back, and {idea}they will not be able to defend themselves{/idea}.
now: You are used to defending yourself: the right words in an argument, a good lawyer, a friend who takes your side. {idea}There is a day when none of that works.{/idea} Building a record with Allah now is the only defense.
old: I can always talk my way out of trouble.
new: On that Day no one defends himself. Only what I did now will help.
try: Seek Allah's forgiveness for one specific thing today.

title: Warned of the fire today. Which favor would you deny?
subtitle: The refrain after the flame and smoke

key.label: Why a warning is a favor

then: Ibn Kathir says Allah's warnings of punishment, like these verses, {idea}should encourage all creatures to abandon disobedience{/idea}. That is {reward}why Allah reminds them of this as a favor{/reward}, right after describing the fire.
now: A smoke alarm going off at 3 a.m. is awful, and it saves your life. {reward}The warning is the kindness{/reward}, not the fire. {idea}These verses are the alarm.{/idea}
old: Verses about the fire are hard to hear, so I skip them.
new: The warning is a mercy that keeps me from what it describes.
try: Next time you hear a warning verse, ask Allah for protection instead of skipping it.

title: When the sky splits and turns red like oil.
subtitle: The heaven itself changes on that Day
then: Ibn Kathir says this is on the Day of Resurrection, when the heaven is {trap}torn and frail{/trap}. It will melt like heated metal and take on colors like dye, red, yellow, blue, green. {idea}This shows the extent of that Day's horrors.{/idea}
now: You look up at a clear blue sky and it feels like the most permanent thing there is. The same sky that 55:7 says He raised. {idea}Even it will change on His command.{/idea}
old: Some things in the world will always be there.
new: Even the sky is temporary. Only Allah does not change.
try: Look at the sky today and remember that it, too, obeys its Lord.

title: Told of the sky's splitting. Which favor would you deny?
subtitle: The refrain after the heaven melts like oil

row.title: a stable sky now
sub: and news of what is coming

then: After the image of {trap}the heaven splitting{/trap}, the refrain comes again. The sky that is whole today is a mercy, and so is being told it will not stay that way, so people can {reward}turn back while there is time{/reward}.
now: You wake up, open the blinds, and the sky is where it was. Another ordinary day. {reward}An ordinary day is time you were given{/reward}, before the Day when the sky does not hold.
old: One more normal day is nothing special.
new: Every day the sky still holds is a respite from my Lord.
try: Use the first ten minutes of tomorrow for something you would be glad to show Allah.

title: On that Day no one will be asked about his sin.
subtitle: A moment when excuses are not even heard
then: Ibn Kathir links it to the verse: {trap}a Day when they shall not speak, nor be allowed to give excuses{/trap}. That is one stage. Later all will be questioned, and Qatadah said {idea}mouths will be sealed and hands and feet will speak{/idea}.
now: You rehearse explanations in your head: I was tired, I was busy, everyone did it. You think you will make your case later. {idea}The time for explaining yourself to Allah is now, in prayer, in tawbah.{/idea}
old: I will explain my reasons when the time comes.
new: There will be a moment with no excuses. The time to speak is now.
try: Tonight, speak to Allah honestly about one mistake, with no excuses.

title: Speak now while you can. Which favor would you deny?
subtitle: The refrain after the silence of that Day
then: After the verse about {trap}a Day with no questions and no excuses{/trap}, the refrain asks again. Ibn Kathir says these warnings are themselves a favor. Being told that the door closes is {reward}an invitation to walk through it while it is open{/reward}.
now: You keep drafting the apology text and deleting it. You keep meaning to make tawbah after Ramadan, after the exams. {reward}Today your words still count.{/reward} {idea}That is a favor not everyone will have later.{/idea}
old: There will always be time to say sorry.
new: Being able to repent today is a favor I should not waste.
try: Send the apology you have been putting off, to a person or to Allah.

title: The guilty will be known by their marks.
subtitle: Deeds show on a person that Day
then: Ibn Kathir says the criminals will be known by {trap}special marks that distinguish them{/trap}, and they will be seized and taken. He contrasts this with the believers, marked by {reward}light on the parts of the body they washed in wudu{/reward}.
now: You do wudu five times a day, sometimes in a rush at a work sink, wiping your arms with a paper towel. {reward}Each time, you are building a light that will show on that Day.{/reward} {idea}Small, repeated acts become your mark.{/idea}
old: What I do in private does not show on me.
new: My deeds will become visible marks. Wudu is a light I am building now.
try: Make your next wudu slowly and with full attention.

title: Your mark is still being made. Which favor would you deny?
subtitle: The refrain after the guilty are known by their marks
then: After describing how the criminals {trap}will be recognized and seized{/trap}, the refrain asks again. Ibn Kathir says these warnings are a favor because they should move people to {reward}abandon disobedience{/reward} while they still can.
now: You think of yourself as a certain kind of person: the angry one, the lazy one, the one who never prays Fajr. {reward}Nothing is sealed yet.{/reward} {idea}Each day you can change what marks you.{/idea}
old: This is just who I am.
new: The mark I carry on that Day is still being made. That is a favor.
try: Choose one small habit that you want to be known for, and do it once today.

title: This is the Hell the criminals denied.
subtitle: What was called a story becomes visible
then: Ibn Kathir explains it is said to them: {trap}this is the Fire you used to deny existed{/trap}, now you see it before your eyes. {idea}What they waved away as a story{/idea} stands in front of them.
now: You do not open the letter from the bank because you do not want to know. You skip the checkup because the news might be bad. {idea}Not looking does not change what is there.{/idea} Facing it early is the only way to do something about it.
old: If I do not think about it, it cannot hurt me.
new: Denying something real only removes my chance to prepare for it.
try: Face one thing today that you have been avoiding looking at.

title: They go round between it and boiling water.
subtitle: No rest for those who denied

row.title: I ask Allah to save me

then: Ibn Kathir says they will go between the fire and {trap}hamim, a drink of intense heat{/trap}. Ibn Abbas said it has reached the ultimate temperature. Ibn Kathir adds that punishing the criminals and favoring the mindful are both {idea}from Allah's justice and mercy{/idea}.
now: You feel that restlessness already in small form: going back and forth between two bad options, no peace in either. {idea}That is a taste of a life lived away from Allah.{/idea} Peace is found by turning to Him.
old: Hellfire is something I do not need to think about.
new: Knowing the punishment is real makes me hold on to Allah's mercy tighter.
try: Ask Allah today, in your own words, to protect you and your family from the Fire.

title: Warned before it is real. Which favor would you deny?
subtitle: The refrain that closes the description of Hell
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah's warnings, {idea}such as mentioned in these verses{/idea}, should encourage all creatures to leave shirk and disobedience, and {reward}this is why Allah reminded them of this favor{/reward} with the refrain.
now: A doctor shows you an X-ray and says: if you keep smoking, this is where it goes. It is hard to look at. {reward}It is also the kindest thing anyone has done for you this year.{/reward}
old: A merciful Lord would not talk about punishment.
new: Telling me clearly what to avoid is part of His mercy.
try: Leave one small sin today, for the sake of the warning you just read.

title: Whoever fears standing before his Lord gets two gardens.
subtitle: The turn from warning to reward
then: Ibn Kathir links it to the verse about one who {idea}restrained himself from desires{/idea}. Such a person knows the Hereafter is better and more lasting, so he does what his Lord ordered. Ibn Kathir says this includes believing jinn, since {reward}both are reminded of this favor{/reward}.
now: Late at night, the phone in your hand, nobody watching. You think for one second: one day I will stand before Allah. You put it down. {reward}That second is what this verse is about.{/reward}
old: Fearing Allah means feeling bad all the time.
new: Remembering I will stand before Him in the moment of choice is what earns gardens.
try: In one moment of temptation today, pause and picture standing before your Lord.

title: Two gardens for one fear. Which favor would you deny?
subtitle: The refrain after the promise of two gardens
then: Ibn Kathir says this verse applies to {idea}both humans and jinn{/idea}, because Allah reminds both of this favor. The Prophet ﷺ described gardens of silver and gardens of gold, and in Adn {reward}nothing stands between the people and looking at their Lord but the covering of His pride{/reward}.
now: You give up a weekend of fun to care for a sick parent. You skip the deal that was not quite honest. It feels like losing. {reward}The exchange rate is two gardens.{/reward}
old: Giving up something for Allah means I lose out.
new: Every desire I leave for Allah is repaid far beyond its worth.
try: Give up one small thing today for Allah's sake, and remember the exchange.

title: Gardens with spreading branches.
subtitle: Trees full of fresh growth and fruit
then: Ibn Kathir says their trees have {reward}beautiful young branches{/reward} that bear every kind of ripe fruit. Ata al-Khurasani said afnan means {idea}branches that spread until they reach the branches of other trees{/idea}.
now: You walk under a row of old trees on a hot day and feel the shade cool your face. The branches meet over the path. {reward}That moment is a tiny hint{/reward} of a garden that never dries.
old: Paradise is too far away to imagine.
new: Every shady tree here is a small sign of the gardens there.
try: Sit under a tree for a few minutes this week and ask Allah for Jannah.

title: Shade and fruit on every branch. Which favor would you deny?
subtitle: The refrain after the spreading branches
then: Right after the {reward}branches that hold every type of ripened fruit{/reward}, the question returns. Ibn Kathir places the refrain after each detail of the gardens: {idea}each gift is named, then the listener is asked{/idea}.
now: You plant a small tree on your balcony and wait two years for the first lemon. You are thrilled by one fruit. {reward}Imagine branches that never stop giving.{/reward} {idea}Your joy at that lemon is a clue.{/idea}
old: I cannot get excited about something I cannot see.
new: The joy I feel at small good things here points to a far greater favor.
try: Water a plant today, or buy one, as a small reminder of the gardens.

title: Two springs flowing freely in them.
subtitle: Water that never stops
then: Ibn Kathir says the springs flow freely to {reward}water the trees and branches{/reward}. Al-Hasan al-Basri said one is called {idea}Tasnim and the other Salsabil{/idea}.
now: You check the water bill and wince. You watch the news about a dry summer and hosepipe bans. {reward}There, the water never stops and never costs.{/reward}
old: Good things always run out eventually.
new: In the gardens, the good flows and does not end.
try: Give someone water today, a glass or a bottle, as a small charity.

title: Springs that never run dry. Which favor would you deny?
subtitle: The refrain after the two flowing springs
then: The refrain follows {reward}two springs flowing{/reward} in the gardens. Each time a gift of Paradise is named, the listener is asked again. Here the gift is {idea}water that never stops{/idea}.
now: You chase the next purchase, the next trip, the next upgrade. Each one quenches you for a day. {idea}This world's water leaves you thirsty again.{/idea} {reward}The springs of the gardens do not.{/reward}
old: The next thing I get will finally satisfy me.
new: Lasting satisfaction is with Allah, not in the next purchase.
try: Skip one purchase you do not need today and put the money toward charity.

title: Every fruit in two kinds.
subtitle: The known, and better than the known
then: Ibn Kathir says there will be every kind of fruit, {reward}what they knew before, and better, and what they never knew{/reward}. Ibn Abbas said, {idea}nothing in this world is in the Hereafter except in name{/idea}, so great is the difference.
now: You remember the best mango you ever ate, on a hot afternoon at your grandmother's house. You still talk about it. {reward}That was the name. The real thing is waiting.{/reward}
old: Paradise will be a nicer version of what I know.
new: What waits there shares only the name with what I know here.
try: Share a piece of fruit with someone today and tell them about this verse.

title: Fruit beyond imagining. Which favor would you deny?
subtitle: The refrain after every fruit in pairs
then: Ibn Kathir says in the gardens there are {reward}delights that no eye has seen, no ear has heard and no heart has imagined{/reward}. After naming fruits in pairs, {idea}the question is asked once more{/idea}.
now: You scroll holiday photos of a place you will never afford. You feel a small ache. {reward}What Allah prepared has no photos, because no eye has seen it.{/reward}
old: I already know what the best things in life look like.
new: The best of Allah's favors is beyond anything I can imagine.
try: Make a dua today asking Allah for what no heart has imagined.

title: Reclining on silk-lined couches, fruit hanging within reach.
subtitle: Rest and ease in the first two gardens
then: Ikrimah and Qatadah said istabraq is {reward}thick silk brocade{/reward}. Ibn Masud said: {idea}this is the lining, so what about the outside?{/idea} Ibn Kathir says the fruit comes down from the branches to whoever wants it, reclining or not.
now: You come home after a twelve-hour shift and fall onto the sofa. Even the remote is too far away. {reward}A rest where everything you want comes to you{/reward} is what this verse describes, after a life of effort.
old: Rest is something I have to earn every day, and it never lasts.
new: The effort of this life ends in a rest where everything is within reach.
try: When you rest tonight, say: O Allah, grant me the rest of the gardens.

title: Rest with fruit in reach. Which favor would you deny?
subtitle: The refrain after the couches and low fruit
then: After describing {reward}couches of brocade and fruit hanging low{/reward}, the refrain asks again. Ibn Kathir cites the verses where the fruit bunches hang low within reach. {idea}Ease is named as a favor in itself.{/idea}
now: You are tired in a way sleep does not fix: caring for a newborn, nursing a parent, two jobs. {idea}Tiredness spent in good is not wasted.{/idea} {reward}It is walking toward a rest that does not end.{/reward}
old: My exhaustion is just the price of life.
new: Tiredness in doing good is a road toward a rest I cannot deny.
try: Offer your tiredness today to Allah, and ask Him to accept it.

title: Companions whose eyes are only for their spouses.
subtitle: Faithfulness as a reward
then: Ibn Abbas and Qatadah said these are {reward}wives who restrain their glances, desiring none but their husbands{/reward}. Ibn Kathir says the verse is also proof that {idea}believing jinn will enter Paradise{/idea}.
now: You see couples who have been together forty years, still holding hands at the bus stop. What moves you is not beauty, it is that they still only see each other. {reward}The verse names faithfulness as a reward.{/reward}
old: Loyalty in love is rare and old-fashioned.
new: Faithfulness is so precious that Allah names it among the rewards of Paradise.
try: Do one small thing today to show loyalty to your spouse or family.

title: A love that looks nowhere else. Which favor would you deny?
subtitle: The refrain after the faithful companions
then: The refrain follows the description of companions {reward}who desire none but their spouses{/reward}. Ibn Kathir reports one will say: by Allah, I see nothing in Paradise more handsome or beloved to me than you, {idea}so praise be to Allah who made you for me{/idea}.
now: You worry about your marriage, or whether you will ever marry, or about a love that went wrong. {reward}A love free of fear is promised{/reward}, and its first words there are praise to Allah.
old: Love always comes with worry and pain.
new: A secure, faithful love is a favor Allah promises.
try: Make a dua today for the marriage of someone you know, or your own.

title: As if they were rubies and coral.
subtitle: Purity and radiance
then: Mujahid and Al-Hasan said they are {reward}as pure as rubies and white as marjan{/reward}, here meaning pearls. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith that the first group to enter Paradise will {idea}look like the moon on a full night{/idea}.
now: You see filters, before-and-after photos, the endless effort to look a certain way. Beauty here fades and needs maintaining. {reward}The beauty described there is like gemstones: it does not wear out.{/reward}
old: Beauty is something you have to chase and protect.
new: The beauty of Paradise is pure and lasting, a gift, not a chase.
try: Compliment someone today on a quality of character, not appearance.

title: Pure as rubies. Which favor would you deny?
subtitle: The refrain after rubies and coral
then: Ibn Kathir cites the hadith of Anas: {reward}a place in Paradise the size of a whip is better than the world and all on it{/reward}. After the image of rubies and coral, {idea}the refrain asks again{/idea}.
now: You spend months saving for a bigger flat, a nicer car. You measure your life in square meters. {reward}A strip of Paradise the length of a whip is worth more than all of it.{/reward}
old: A bigger place here would make me happy.
new: The smallest place in Paradise is worth more than the whole world.
try: Before you buy something big this week, ask yourself what it is worth next to Jannah.

title: Is the reward for good anything but good?
subtitle: Ihsan answered with ihsan
then: Ibn Kathir says only good is the fitting reward for those who do good, citing: {reward}for those who did good is the best, and more{/reward}. He adds these blessings {idea}cannot be earned merely by deeds, but by Allah's favor and bounty{/idea}.
now: You hold the door, you cover a colleague's shift, you call your mother when you would rather not. Nobody thanks you. {idea}The verse asks a question that already holds its answer.{/idea} {reward}Good comes back as good.{/reward}
old: Doing good just means people take advantage of me.
new: Good is never lost. Allah answers it with good, and more.
try: Do one act of ihsan today, a little more than what is required.

title: Good repaid with good. Which favor would you deny?
subtitle: The refrain after the reward of ihsan
then: Ibn Kathir says all these blessings are {reward}tremendous{/reward}, given by Allah's favor rather than earned by deeds alone. {idea}After all of these, He asks again{/idea}: which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?
now: You did something good last week and felt a small glow of pride. {idea}Even the chance to do it was His gift{/idea}, and so is His accepting it. {reward}Favor on top of favor.{/reward}
old: My good deeds are my own achievement.
new: That Allah lets me do good, and then rewards it, is a double favor.
try: After your next good deed, say Alhamdulillah for being allowed to do it.

title: And below those two, two more gardens.
subtitle: Paradise has levels

row.title: two more
sub: silver, for those on the right

then: Ibn Kathir says these gardens are {idea}lower in virtue and status{/idea} than the first two. Abu Musa said: {reward}two gardens of gold for the muqarrabin, two of silver for the people of the right{/reward}.
now: You think you will never be one of the very best: the night-prayer people, the ones who memorized it all. {reward}There is a garden for those on the right too.{/reward} {idea}And you can still aim higher.{/idea}
old: If I cannot be the best, there is no place for me.
new: Paradise has levels: room to be saved, and room to rise higher.
try: Pick one small extra deed to aim a level higher this week.

title: A garden for every level. Which favor would you deny?
subtitle: The refrain after the second pair of gardens

row.title: also for those on the right

then: Ibn Kathir says the first two gardens are for {idea}the near ones{/idea}, and these for {reward}the people of the right{/reward}. Even the lower rank is a pair of gardens, and the refrain asks again which favor would be denied.
now: You compare yourself to the most pious person you know and feel hopeless. {reward}Allah made room for people who are trying, not only for those who have arrived.{/reward}
old: I am not good enough for Paradise.
new: Allah prepared gardens for ordinary believers too. That is a favor.
try: Tell yourself one thing you do well for Allah, and ask Him to accept it.

title: Dark green, deep with water.
subtitle: Gardens so watered they look almost black
then: Ibn Abbas said mudhammatan means {reward}they have become dark green because of extensive watering{/reward}. Muhammad bin Kab said it means {idea}full of greenery{/idea}.
now: You fly over a desert and suddenly see a field of deep green where a river runs. Your eye goes straight to it. {reward}Green that deep means life.{/reward}
old: One shade of green is like another.
new: Even the color of the gardens speaks of endless life and water.
try: Find the greenest thing near you today and look at it for a minute with gratitude.

title: Deep green life. Which favor would you deny?
subtitle: The refrain after the dark green gardens
then: After the image of gardens {reward}dark green from abundant water{/reward}, the refrain returns. For the first listeners in a dry land, {idea}deep green was the picture of wealth and life{/idea}.
now: You watch your lawn or your potted plants turn brown in a heatwave, and you water them every evening anyway. {reward}There is a garden that never needs saving.{/reward}
old: Everything green eventually dries up.
new: The gardens Allah promises stay green forever.
try: Water a plant or a tree today and say: O Allah, make my place green in Jannah.

title: Two springs gushing in them.
subtitle: Water that wells up without end

picture.label: Two pairs, two kinds of springs

then: Ibn Abbas said naddakhatan means {reward}gushing{/reward}, and that free flowing is stronger than gushing, which is why the first gardens are higher. Ad-Dahhak said these springs are {idea}full of water and constantly gushing{/idea}.
now: You turn on a weak shower on a cold morning and wish for pressure. You see a fountain in a park and kids running through it. {reward}Even the lower gardens have springs that never stop.{/reward}
old: A lower rank in Paradise would hardly be worth it.
new: Even the lower gardens overflow. Every level is more than I deserve.
try: Thank Allah today for one ordinary thing, like hot water, by name.

title: Springs that keep welling up. Which favor would you deny?
subtitle: The refrain after the gushing springs
then: After the {reward}two springs constantly gushing{/reward}, as Ad-Dahhak described them, the refrain returns. The surah asks the question {idea}after every single gift{/idea}, even in the lower gardens.
now: You notice Allah's gifts in your life come like that too: not once, but again and again. Another pay cheque, another healthy morning, another chance. {reward}It keeps welling up.{/reward}
old: I got my share of blessings already.
new: Allah's favors keep welling up. I cannot deny even one of them.
try: Count the blessings you received just this morning, before noon.

title: Fruit, date palms and pomegranates.
subtitle: Familiar fruits named in the second gardens
then: Ibn Kathir compares this to the first gardens, which have {reward}every kind of fruit in pairs{/reward}. He says that description is better, with more variety. Here, dates and pomegranates are named: {idea}fruits the first listeners knew and loved{/idea}.
now: You break your fast with a date in Ramadan. You split a pomegranate in autumn and your fingers turn red. {reward}Allah names the fruits you already love{/reward}, so the promise feels close.
old: Paradise is too strange for me to picture.
new: Allah describes Paradise with things I know, so I can long for it.
try: Eat a date or a pomegranate this week and ask Allah for the gardens.

title: Dates and pomegranates waiting. Which favor would you deny?
subtitle: The refrain after the fruits of the second gardens
then: After naming {reward}dates and pomegranates{/reward}, the refrain returns. These were fruits of the land, and Ibn Abbas said nothing in the Hereafter matches this world {idea}except in name{/idea}.
now: You buy a box of dates at the market without thinking. Next time, hold one and remember: {reward}this is the name of something waiting for you.{/reward}
old: Fruit here has nothing to do with the Hereafter.
new: Every date I eat is a small reminder of a promised favor.
try: Say Bismillah and Alhamdulillah over the next fruit you eat, slowly.

title: In them are good and beautiful ones.
subtitle: Goodness of character named with beauty
then: Qatadah said it means {reward}various good and delightful things{/reward} in the gardens. Most scholars said khayrah is {idea}a righteous, well-mannered, beautiful woman{/idea}, and Ibn Kathir says this is also reported from Umm Salamah from the Prophet ﷺ.
now: You meet someone stunning who is unkind to waiters, and the beauty disappears. You meet someone plain who is gentle with everyone, and they glow. {reward}Goodness is named first.{/reward}
old: Looks are the first thing that matters.
new: Goodness of character is the beauty that is named first.
try: Work on one good manner today, like patience or a kind word.

title: Goodness and beauty together. Which favor would you deny?
subtitle: The refrain after the good and beautiful ones
then: After {reward}khayrat hisan{/reward}, good and beautiful companions, the refrain asks again. The gift is not only beauty but {idea}good character{/idea}, company that is kind and well-mannered.
now: You have one friend who always makes you better: calls you to pray, forgives fast, laughs easily. {reward}Good company here is a taste of the favor there.{/reward}
old: Friends are just people I happen to know.
new: Good company is a favor Allah names even in Paradise.
try: Message one good friend today and thank them for who they are.

title: Fair companions, sheltered in pavilions.
subtitle: Honor and privacy in tents of pearl
then: Ibn Kathir cites the hadith in Al-Bukhari: in Paradise the believer will have {reward}a tent from a hollow pearl, sixty miles wide{/reward}. He compares this verse with 55:56 and says {idea}those who restrain their own glances are better{/idea}, though both are secluded.
now: You live in a world that films everything: dinners, arguments, children's tears, all posted. {reward}What is precious is protected.{/reward} {idea}Not everything beautiful needs an audience.{/idea}
old: If it is not shared, it is not valued.
new: In Paradise, what is precious is kept honored and private.
try: Keep one beautiful moment today offline, just between you and your family.

title: Pavilions of pearl. Which favor would you deny?
subtitle: The refrain after the sheltered pavilions
then: Ibn Kathir describes the pavilion as {reward}a tent made of a single hollow pearl{/reward}, sixty miles long in Muslim's narration. Then the refrain: {idea}which of your Lord's favors would you deny?{/idea}
now: You scroll property listings and sigh at prices. Your flat is cramped, the neighbors are loud. {reward}A home of pearl is being kept for the believer.{/reward} {idea}This one is a waiting room.{/idea}
old: My home will never be what I want.
new: The home I long for is promised. This one is temporary.
try: Thank Allah today for the roof you have, however small.

title: Untouched by any human or jinn before them.
subtitle: A gift made new, only for you

key.label: What it says about the gift

then: Ibn Kathir says {idea}this meaning was explained before{/idea}, at 55:56: a purity kept only for the believer. He notes the earlier verse is also {reward}proof that believing jinn enter Paradise{/reward}, each with their own kind.
now: You remember the joy of something brand new, made just for you: a hand-knitted jumper, a cake with your name on it. {reward}Allah's gift to the believer is prepared for them alone.{/reward}
old: Everything good has already been used by someone else.
new: Allah prepares gifts in Paradise kept only for the one who receives them.
try: Make or give something today made just for one person you love.

title: A gift kept only for you. Which favor would you deny?
subtitle: The refrain after the untouched companions
then: This refrain repeats the one after 55:56, with {idea}the same description of purity{/idea} now for the second gardens. Even those on the right receive {reward}a gift kept for them alone{/reward}.
now: You often feel generic: a number at work, a face in the queue, a username. {reward}Allah's reward is personal, prepared for you by name.{/reward}
old: Nobody prepares anything just for me.
new: Allah has prepared gifts with my name on them. That is a favor I cannot deny.
try: Ask Allah in your own words today for the gift He has prepared for you.

title: Reclining on green cushions and fine carpets.
subtitle: The last scene of the gardens
then: Ibn Abbas and others said rafraf means {reward}cushions{/reward}, arranged over the couches. Abqariy means {reward}rich carpets{/reward}. Ibn Kathir compares these with the first gardens' couches of brocade, where {idea}the lining alone was silk{/idea}.
now: You save for months for a good sofa, or you sit on a thin rug at the mosque with sore knees. {reward}Comfort is coming that no shop sells.{/reward}
old: Comfort is what I can afford.
new: The comfort Allah prepares is beyond what money can buy.
try: Sit on your prayer mat today a few extra minutes after salah, just to remember Allah.

title: The last refrain: which favor would you deny?
subtitle: After the full journey from creation to the gardens
then: This is the last time the question is asked, after {reward}green cushions and fine carpets{/reward}. Ibn Kathir says we answer as the believing jinn did: {idea}O Allah, none of Your favors do we deny, all praise is Yours{/idea}.
now: You have heard this question again and again through the surah. Each time about something different: your tongue, the sea, a ship, a warning, a garden. {idea}Now answer it once, for all of them.{/idea}
old: I have heard this verse so many times it blurs together.
new: Each repeat was about a different favor. My answer covers all of them.
try: Say out loud today: none of Your favors do I deny, my Lord, all praise is Yours.

title: Blessed is the name of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honor.
subtitle: The surah ends where every favor comes from
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah is worthy of being {idea}remembered and never forgotten, appreciated and never unappreciated{/idea}. The Prophet ﷺ said: persist in calling Ya Dhal-Jalal wal-Ikram. After salah he would say: {reward}O Allah, You are As-Salam, blessed are You, Owner of Majesty and Honor{/reward}.
now: You finish your prayer and reach for your phone in the same second. {idea}The Prophet ﷺ stayed a moment.{/idea} Those few words after salam are where this whole surah lands.
old: The prayer is over once I say salam.
new: Every favor points back to His name. I end, as the surah does, by blessing it.
try: After your next prayer, say: Allahumma antas-Salam wa minkas-salam, tabarakta ya Dhal-Jalali wal-Ikram.
